parsed.hook: The Richard Dinner Vineyard sits above the morning fog line on Sonoma Mountain's eastern slopes, where volcanic and rocky loam soils and sharp diurnal swings produce Chardonnay with more tension than the typical Sonoma Coast bottling. Paul Hobbs has been farming this site for decades, and the Cuvée Agustina — named for his mother — is where he puts his best fruit from it.
parsed.wine_summary:
Sonoma Mountain is a small, elevated AVA that most Chardonnay drinkers walk past on the shelf. At 400 to 2,295 feet, the mountain sits above the fog that blankets the Sonoma Valley floor each morning, meaning vines get more direct sun exposure but also more dramatic temperature swings — sometimes 50°F between day and night. That diurnal range is the key variable: it slows ripening, preserves natural acidity, and keeps alcohol from climbing unchecked. The result is Chardonnay that ripens fully but holds its shape.

Paul Hobbs built his reputation through obsessive site selection and a winemaking philosophy borrowed heavily from Burgundy — small lots, vineyard-specific bottlings, minimal intervention where the fruit is strong enough to carry the wine. The Cuvée Agustina is the top expression from the Dinner Vineyard, which Hobbs has sourced from long enough to understand its rhythms. The TEXSOM track record here is consistent: gold medals in 2014, 2015, and 2016 suggest the wine performs best in warmer, riper vintages, while 2017 and 2021 — both cooler and more challenging years in Sonoma — earned silvers. That pattern tells you something real about where this wine's ceiling is.
parsed.terroir_expression: The Dinner Vineyard's volcanic and rocky loam soils drain quickly, forcing vine roots to work harder and deeper for water and nutrients — a stress that concentrates flavor without inflating sugar levels. Volcanic soils tend to produce wines with a savory, almost mineral edge that distinguishes them from the rounder profiles you get off alluvial valley floor sites. The elevation above the fog line means longer daily sun exposure than lower Sonoma Mountain vineyards, which pushes phenolic ripeness, but the cold nights pull that back toward freshness. In the glass, this translates to stone fruit — white peach, nectarine — with a structural backbone of citrus acidity and a flinty, slightly smoky undercurrent that is the volcanic soil's direct contribution.
parsed.vinification_summary: Hobbs works in a Burgundian framework: whole-cluster pressing, barrel fermentation in French oak (a mix of new and neutral), and extended lees aging with periodic bâtonnage — stirring the spent yeast cells back into the wine to add texture and roundness. Malolactic fermentation, which converts sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, is likely employed here, as it is in virtually all serious California Chardonnay, but Hobbs tends to calibrate it rather than let it run completely unchecked, which is why the wine retains a lively acid line rather than going fully creamy and flat. The percentage of new oak is not publicly disclosed for this bottling, but the style suggests moderate new oak use — enough to add vanilla and toasty complexity without overwhelming the site's natural character.
parsed.food_pairing:
1. Roast chicken with tarragon butter — the classic pairing for a reason. The wine's stone fruit and oak-derived richness mirror the fat in the butter while its acidity cuts through the skin. Nothing more complicated needed.
2. Lobster roll (Connecticut style, warm with drawn butter) — the lactic richness of the wine and the sweetness of fresh lobster amplify each other; the acidity keeps it from feeling heavy.
3. Pan-seared halibut with brown butter and capers — the brown butter echoes the wine's toasty, nutty oak notes; the capers introduce a briny sharpness that plays against the fruit.
4. Truffle risotto — Sonoma Mountain Chardonnay with its savory volcanic edge is one of the few whites that doesn't get lost next to truffle's intensity; the wine's body holds up.
5. Triple-cream brie with honeycomb on a board — for casual drinking, the wine's richness and slight sweetness of fruit work against the salt and fat of the cheese without needing a formal table.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Kistler Les Noisetiers Chardonnay — also Sonoma-sourced, also Burgundian in method, similarly priced. The Kistler tends toward more obvious oak and cream; the Dinner Vineyard has more mineral definition from the volcanic site.
DuMOL Clare Chardonnay (Russian River Valley) — comparable price point and quality tier, with more citrus and less stone fruit due to the cooler Russian River site. A useful reference if you want to understand how much Sonoma Mountain elevation actually changes the flavor equation.
Littorai Mays Canyon Chardonnay — slightly leaner and more Chablis-inflected, but shares the commitment to site specificity and restrained winemaking. If the Dinner Vineyard feels too rich, Littorai is the next step toward austerity.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry white with bright acidity, stone fruit depth, and a mineral, slightly smoky finish from volcanic soils
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink between 3 and 8 years from vintage. The 2021 is approachable now but will gain complexity through 2026–2027. Store at 55°F in a dark, vibration-free environment; this wine will not benefit from being opened too young if you have the patience.
parsed.value_assessment: This wine typically retails between $60 and $80 depending on vintage and retailer. At that price, it sits alongside Kistler Sonoma Mountain Chardonnay and Aubert Lauren Vineyard Chardonnay, both of which carry more critical heat and sometimes command premiums. The Dinner Vineyard is not underpriced, but the TEXSOM gold medals in three consecutive vintages and the specificity of the single-vineyard sourcing make it a defensible buy at the top of that range — particularly in warmer years where the site fully delivers.
parsed.market_position: This bottle lands primarily on restaurant wine lists in the $120–$160 range and in specialty retail shops that carry a serious California Chardonnay section. The audience is the Chardonnay buyer who has moved past mass-market Napa Chardonnay and wants site-specific bottlings but isn't yet hunting for Burgundy grand cru. Collectors pick it up in case quantities in strong vintages; casual drinkers encounter it mostly on by-the-glass programs at higher-end restaurants.
parsed.insider_take: The comparison to Burgundy that Hobbs courts is real in method but not in style — this is a richer, more voluptuous wine than a Puligny-Montrachet, and buyers expecting Meursault-level restraint will be surprised. The volcanic mineral character is the wine's most interesting feature and the thing most people miss when they focus on the oak and fruit. If you're buying across vintages, prioritize 2014, 2015, and 2016 over 2017 and 2021 — the warmer years are where this site's personality comes through most clearly.
